abstract: Future coral reef persistence amidst accelerating climate change depends on rapid adaptive capacity. Sixteen years (2003 to 2019) of genetic data (N = 903) spanning mass mortality events uncovered polygenic signals of evolution and population structure in one Great Barrier Reef coral species (Acropora tenuis) and a similar but nonsignificant trend in another (Acropora millepora). Random forest revealed larger genetic shifts postbleaching compared to other time points, which was further supported by critical transitions in 34 years of remotely sensed thermal data (1985 to 2018). Concordant signals across multiple genomic ordinations confirmed significant shifts postbleaching. Specifically, three genetic variants contributed significantly to key random forest splits over time in A. tenuis. Significant genome-wide covariance in allele frequencies suggests shifts due to selection, not drift. This suggests that coral gene pools are changing, and measurable evolution can happen over subdecadal timescales, giving hope for coral resilience amid the ongoing climate crisis. However, we caution against overoptimism, and stress emissions must be urgently reduced.
